logistic_regression.summary: A single weighted vote across your features — a scale that tips toward up or down.

native.produces: A probability of each class for every bar, read by passing one weighted sum of the bar's features through the sigmoid curve.
native.targetVariable: The class label of the bar, for example whether the coming move is up or down, stated as a probability of the up class
native.objectiveNote: The specification adds a squared-size penalty on the weights to the negative log-likelihood, so the weighted sum is deliberately shrunk and the stated odds are a little less extreme than an unpenalised fit would give.

metrics.why: The solver moves the weights of the single weighted sum to make exactly this number small on the training bars, so on unseen bars it is the direct test of whether the sigmoid's stated odds are honest.
metrics.baseline: The logarithmic loss of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: It grades the same sigmoid output on a bounded squared scale, so a handful of bars where the weighted sum ran far from zero cannot dominate the verdict the way they can in the logarithmic score.
metrics.baseline: The Brier score of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: Regressing the outcome on the model's own log-odds, which here is simply the weighted sum, shows whether the weight penalty left the sum too flat or whether correlated indicators made it too steep.
metrics.baseline: A slope of one, the mathematical value for log-odds on the right scale

metrics.why: The sigmoid never reorders bars, so this number tests the weighted sum alone: whether a straight-line blend of the features places up bars above down bars at all.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value when the weighted sum orders up bars and down bars no better than a coin

metrics.why: The straight decision boundary where the weighted sum crosses zero is the model's hard call, and averaging the hit rate of each side stops a boundary that calls nearly every bar one way from looking skilled.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value of calling every bar the same side

metrics.why: A heavily penalised weight vector collapses the weighted sum toward its intercept, and the spread of the stated probabilities shows whether the features move the output at all.
With one weight per feature the only way this model memorises is through too weak a penalty, and the gap between the same log-likelihood on validation rows and on training rows shows it directly.
metrics.baseline: Zero, no gap between the two spans

notApplicable.name: Macro F1-Score
notApplicable.why: It is a hard-call number of the as-run scoreboard that depends on where the sigmoid output is cut; natively the model is judged on its stated odds and its hard call is covered by balanced accuracy.

notApplicable.name: High-Conviction Precision
notApplicable.why: No registry metric restricts scoring to the most confident tenth of bars, and the threshold-free ranking and calibration metrics already test whether large weighted sums are more reliable.

notApplicable.name: Price forecast root mean square error
notApplicable.why: The sigmoid of a weighted sum states a probability of a class and never a size of move, so there is no forecast in points to measure an error on.

notApplicable.name: Sharpe ratio
notApplicable.why: Natively the model only states odds; a Sharpe ratio appears only after the engine turns those odds into positions and charges costs, so it belongs to the as-run layer.

asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the sigmoid of the weighted sum of the bar's features standardised with the training rows' mean and deviation, from a fit in which up bars and down bars each carry half the loss.

meaningful.why: The solver gave up bars and down bars equal weight, so the sigmoid's output is centred on an even prior and this half-and-half logarithmic score is the one that matches what the weights were actually fitted to do; its reference is the natural logarithm of two.
Class weighting shifts the intercept but does not reorder bars, so this is the clean test of whether the weighted sum of features ranks bars that went up above bars that went down.

The engine goes long when the weighted sum is at or above zero and short otherwise, and this is what that straight decision boundary earned after costs beyond simply holding the same contract through the same folds.
It is the money made by trading the sign of the weighted sum under the engine's fill and exit rule with costs charged, read beside the predicted up share and the trade count.
It relates the per-bar profit of following the decision boundary to its bumpiness; zero is only an arithmetic marker because a coin-flip trader still pays costs.
It shows the deepest hole dug while the weighted sum stayed on the wrong side of zero, which a single linear boundary can do for long stretches when the market's regime changes.
It compares the winning trades opened by a flip of the weighted sum's sign with the losing ones after costs; one is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level.
It counts how many of the trades that began when the weighted sum changed sign closed with a profit, which must be read with the average win and loss because exits follow the engine's rule.
It is the hit rate of the call at the zero crossing of the weighted sum; because the fit was class balanced, that crossing sits at an even prior and not at the fold's own up share.
It averages the hit rate on up bars and on down bars, which is the hard-call number that matches a boundary deliberately placed by a fit that weighted the two sides equally.
It condenses the four counts of called against actual direction at the zero crossing into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the boundary merely calls one side most of the time.

The plain logarithmic loss charges the sigmoid's output against the real up share, which the balanced fit did not aim at, so it reads a little worse than the model's ranking deserves; it is also the quantity whose validation value picked the kept solver pass.
It grades the same balanced-prior probability on a bounded squared scale, so it carries the same small penalty for the shifted intercept but cannot be dominated by a few extreme weighted sums.
Class weighting moves the intercept and leaves the steepness alone, so the slope still tells whether the penalised weighted sum is too flat or too steep as log-odds.
It shows whether the regularization strength dial left the weights large enough for the sigmoid output to move away from one half at all.
Both logged curves hold the plain logarithmic loss of the sigmoid output, so their gap at the kept solver pass is a fair overfit check for this model.
It is the score on inner blocks of the training span that chose the regularization strength; it is a selection score, optimistic by construction, and not a result.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The balanced fit centres the sigmoid output on an even prior, so its gap from the observed up share in each bin is partly built in by design and does not show a fault of the weights.
The forecast line comes from a separately fitted ridge regression on the scaled move, not from the logistic weights, so this number says nothing about the classifier.
It measures the miss of the separate ridge price model drawn beside the classifier, whose weights share nothing with the sigmoid's weighted sum.
It is the sign hit rate of the separate ridge forecast, which can disagree with the logistic call on any bar and is never traded.

caveats: The price forecast shown for this model is a second model, a ridge regression whose penalty is the reciprocal of the regularization strength, fitted on the volatility-scaled move with its training target clipped at extreme training percentiles.
The fit runs in ten warm-started solver passes and keeps the pass with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, so the validation logarithmic loss of the kept pass is optimistic.
The logged training curve is the plain logarithmic loss of the sigmoid output, while the solver itself minimised the class-weighted and penalised version of it.
The specification does not mention class weighting; the runnable model always balances the two classes, so a probability of one half means above an even prior and not above the fold's up share.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so intervals around any score need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
For any root other than the micro Nasdaq contract the cost per side is that contract's account figure applied as a stated assumption.

stochastic_gradient_descent.summary: A logistic model trained a few bars at a time, nudging its weights after each small batch — the way neural networks learn.
stochastic_gradient_descent.implementationNote: scikit-learn SGDClassifier with log loss (so it gives probabilities); the price model is SGDRegressor. Plain scikit-learn SGD; the neural models use AdamW.

penalty_strength.label: Penalty strength
penalty_strength.description: How hard the model is pushed toward small coefficients; larger is simpler.

penalty_type.label: Penalty type
penalty_type.description: Which size penalty is used: squared weights (L2), absolute weights (L1, can switch features off) or a mix (elastic net).

l1_penalty_share.label: L1 share of the penalty
l1_penalty_share.description: With the elastic-net penalty: how much of it is L1 (absolute weights) rather than L2.

epochs.label: Epochs
epochs.description: How many passes over the training bars at most.

patience.label: Patience (epochs)
patience.description: Stop after this many epochs without a better validation loss; the best epoch is kept.

native.produces: A linear model whose weights were nudged after every single row or small batch, giving for each feature row the sigmoid of a weighted sum as the probability of the positive class, or the weighted sum itself when the regression loss is chosen.
native.targetVariable: The probability that a feature row belongs to the positive class, which on this dashboard is the close label horizon bars ahead finishing above this bar's close.
native.objectiveNote: Stochastic gradient descent is the update rule and not a model of its own: the specification lets the same row-by-row weight nudges minimise logarithmic loss for a classifier or squared error for a regression, each with a penalty on the size of the weights, and the classification form is the one assigned here.

metrics.why: With the logistic loss chosen, every weight nudge moves the line downhill on exactly this quantity plus the weight penalty, so the same number on unseen rows says whether the noisy row-by-row walk ended somewhere that states honest odds.
metrics.baseline: The logarithmic loss of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar.

metrics.why: The sigmoid of the weighted sum is graded as a squared miss between zero and one, which keeps a handful of rows with a very large weighted sum from deciding the verdict the way they can under the logarithm.
metrics.baseline: The Brier score of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar.

metrics.why: The weight penalty shrinks the weighted sum and stopping the passes early leaves it short, so the slope shows whether the line's log-odds are stretched too far or squeezed toward even odds.
metrics.baseline: A slope of one, which is the mathematical value for log-odds on the right scale.

metrics.why: It asks only whether rows with a larger weighted sum turned out positive more often, so it grades the direction of the learned weight vector without caring how the penalty scaled it.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value of an ordering that carries no information.

metrics.why: A strong weight penalty pulls every coefficient toward zero until the sigmoid quotes nearly the same odds on every row, and this spread shows whether the line still commits to anything.

Because the method is defined by its noisy single-row updates, the logarithmic loss after each pass over the training rows is the only way to see whether the step size let the weights settle or left them bouncing.

The logarithmic loss of the kept pass on later rows minus on the rows it was nudged on shows whether the line memorised its training span, which a linear model does only when the penalty is weak and the features are many.
metrics.baseline: Zero, meaning the line scores the same on rows it was fitted on and rows it never saw.

notApplicable.name: Realized Sharpe Ratio
notApplicable.why: The row-by-row weight nudges produce odds and take no position, so natively this never applied; the as-run layer reports the engine's Sharpe ratio of the fitted line's calls.

notApplicable.name: Annualized Alpha
notApplicable.why: No benchmark and no beta are fitted by the update rule or by the engine, so an alpha was never a quantity this method could output.

notApplicable.name: Maximum Drawdown
notApplicable.why: It is a property of the traded equity path under the engine's rule, reported as run, and tells nothing about whether the noisy updates settled on honest odds.

notApplicable.name: Portfolio Turnover
notApplicable.why: The method fits one weight vector and holds no portfolio; the nearest real quantity is the as-run count of trades per session day.

notApplicable.name: Calmar Ratio
notApplicable.why: It is the engine's return divided by the engine's drawdown, both as-run quantities of the traded calls and neither produced by mini-batch gradient steps.

notApplicable.name: CVaR (99% Tail Risk)
notApplicable.why: The method returns weights and a loss trajectory and never a distribution of trading losses, and the registry has no tail-loss metric for this row.

notApplicable.name: Gaussian negative log-likelihood
notApplicable.why: The logistic form states a probability of a class and never a bell curve around a forecast move, so there is no density to evaluate at the realised move.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-adjusted root mean square error
notApplicable.why: A size-of-move error belongs to the squared-error regression form, which as run is a second, separately fitted line and not the classifier whose odds are being judged.

notApplicable.name: Sharpe ratio
notApplicable.why: Natively the method outputs odds and takes no position, so a reward-for-risk figure grades the engine's trading rule and costs and exists only on the as-run layer.

notApplicable.name: Relative optimality gap
notApplicable.why: The noisy updates carry no proven bound on how far the kept weights are from the best possible weights, so there is no certificate to report.

asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the up-class column of predict_proba from a scikit-learn stochastic gradient descent classifier with the logistic loss, that is the sigmoid of a weighted sum of the standardised features, with no class weighting and no curve fitted on top.

meaningful.why: The classifier was nudged row by row on unweighted logarithmic loss, so on the test walk this is the model's own objective measured where neither the weights nor the kept epoch ever saw the bars.
The weighted sum is continuous, so this is a fair test of whether bars the line scored higher went up more often over the label horizon, whatever the penalty did to the scale of the weights.
It grades the sigmoid of the weighted sum as a squared miss, a bounded second opinion on the same odds that a few extreme feature rows cannot dominate.

Because the fit is unweighted, the sigmoid output is a real frequency claim against the base rate, and the binned gap shows whether a stated chance of up matched the observed up share; it is read with the occupied-bin count because a penalised line keeps its odds close to even.
It shows without bins whether the penalty and the early-kept epoch left the line's log-odds too flat or too steep on the test bars.
It shows how far the sigmoid output moves away from its average, which collapses toward nothing when the search picks a large penalty_strength.

The training and validation curves both hold the plain logarithmic loss of the same probabilities, so the kept epoch's difference between them is a clean reading of how much the line fitted its own span.

It is the share of scored bars where the sigmoid landed on the right side of one half, and because the fit is unweighted that cut carries the training base rate, so it is read beside the majority-class accuracy of the same fold.
It shows whether the learned weights added anything to the line's own intercept, which alone would call the fold's training majority direction on every bar.
It averages how often the line caught the up bars and how often it caught the down bars, so a model that leans on its intercept and calls one side nearly always earns no credit.
It sums up the four cells of the line's hard calls in one symmetric number that stays near zero when the weighted sum only echoes the training base rate.
It is what the sign of the line's call earned after costs under the engine's rule of following the latest call and filling at the next bar's open, read beside buy and hold on the same folds.
It is the per-bar reward for risk of trading the line's call under the engine's rule and costs, and it depends only on which side of one half the sigmoid fell, never on how confident it was.
It is the deepest fall of the equity made by trading the line's call, which shows what a fixed set of weights costs when the test bars stop behaving like the training span.
It compares dollars won with dollars lost over the closed trades the line's flips produced, after costs, as a description of the engine's rule applied to this model's calls.
It is the share of closed trades that ended positive, where a trade ends when the line's call changes side, a stop or target is hit or the fold ends, so it is read with the trade count.
It shows how often the line called up, which exposes a heavily penalised model whose intercept decides nearly every bar.
It counts how often the line's call switched side or a trade otherwise ended, which is needed to read every trading number of a model whose weighted sum hovers near zero.

It grades a second, separately fitted stochastic gradient descent regressor trained on squared error against forecasting no move on the same resolved bars; it says nothing about the classifier's odds.
It is the typical miss in points of the separately fitted regression line after tick rounding, read beside the no-change forecast's error on the same bars.

It is how often the sign of the regression line's forecast matched the actual move on bars where both are non-zero after tick rounding; it belongs to the regressor and can disagree with the traded call.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The classifier is fitted without class weights, so its odds are centred on the training base rate and the score that gives each class half the weight would grade it against a target it never aimed at.
With long_only off and no stop or target the engine is always long or short once the first call is made, so the share of bars in a position describes the engine's rule and not the line.
It is the selection score that picked penalty_strength, penalty_type and l1_penalty_share inside the training span, optimistic by construction and not a result of the fitted line.

caveats: The kept epoch is the one with the lowest validation logarithmic loss, so the validation figure is optimistic and only the test walk is out of sample.

The price line is a second model, a stochastic gradient descent regressor whose kept epoch is chosen on validation mean absolute error, so the forecast metrics and the direction metrics grade two different sets of weights.
The training and validation curves hold the logarithmic loss without the weight penalty, so they are not the full penalised objective the updates followed.

probit_regression.summary: Like logistic regression, but the weighted vote becomes a probability through the normal bell curve instead of the logistic curve.
probit_regression.implementationNote: statsmodels Probit. It has no regression form, so this model draws no forecast line.

max_iterations.label: Maximum iterations
max_iterations.description: The most steps the solver takes to find the weights.

native.produces: A probability of the positive class for every bar, read by passing one weighted sum of the features through the cumulative curve of the standard normal distribution.
native.targetVariable: The binary class label of the bar, for example a buy or sell signal, stated as a probability of the positive class
native.objectiveNote: The model imagines a hidden score equal to the weighted sum plus standard normal noise and calls the bar positive when that score is above zero, and the specification adds a squared-size penalty on the weights.

metrics.why: The weights are chosen to maximise the log of the normal-curve probability given to what happened, so this number on unseen bars is the fitted likelihood out of sample; the thin tails of the normal curve make a confident miss especially expensive here.
metrics.baseline: The logarithmic loss of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: Because the normal curve reaches near-certainty faster than the sigmoid does, a bounded squared score is needed beside the logarithmic one to see whether a few extreme hidden scores are driving the result.
metrics.baseline: The Brier score of quoting the fold's training up share on every scored bar

metrics.why: It checks whether the unit-variance noise assumed for the hidden score matches the market: a slope away from one says the normal curve is turning the weighted sum into odds that are too bold or too timid.
metrics.baseline: A slope of one, the mathematical value for log-odds on the right scale

metrics.why: The normal curve is monotone, so this number tests only the hidden score: whether the straight-line blend of features sits higher on positive bars than on negative ones.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value when the hidden score orders the two classes no better than a coin

metrics.why: The hard call is the sign of the hidden score, and averaging the hit rate over the two sides shows whether that straight boundary separates them or simply sits on one side of nearly every bar.
metrics.baseline: One half, the value of calling every bar the same side

metrics.why: When the penalty shrinks every weight the hidden score stops moving and the normal curve returns almost the same probability on every bar, which this spread exposes.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is a real probit fitted by maximum likelihood on the up or down label, but when its penalty strength is above zero it uses an absolute-value penalty where the specification writes a squared-size penalty, it covers only the binary case, and it has no price model; the as-run numbers measure the binary probit's own probability of up.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the standard normal cumulative curve applied to an intercept plus the weighted sum of features standardised with the training rows' mean and deviation, from an unweighted maximum-likelihood fit with no curve added afterwards.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per bar, one value for the single fit; both numbers are the plain logarithmic loss of the normal-curve probability of up, on the training rows and on the validation rows, and neither includes the absolute-value penalty term

meaningful.why: The weights were fitted by maximising the unweighted log of the normal-curve probability given to each training label, so this is the same quantity on unseen bars and the direct test of the stated odds; the thin normal tails make a confident miss costly.
The normal curve never reorders bars, so this tests the hidden score alone: whether the weighted sum of features sits higher on bars that went up than on bars that went down.
The engine goes long when the hidden score is at or above zero and short otherwise, and this is what that straight boundary earned after costs beyond holding the same contract through the same folds.
It is the money made by trading the sign of the hidden score under the engine's fill and exit rule with costs charged, read beside the predicted up share and the trade count.
It relates the per-bar profit of following the sign of the hidden score to its bumpiness; zero is only an arithmetic marker because a coin-flip trader still pays costs.

It shows the deepest loss run while the hidden score stayed on the wrong side of zero; an unweighted fit follows the training up share, so in a one-sided training span the boundary can sit on one side for long stretches.
It compares winning with losing trades opened when the hidden score changed sign, after costs; one is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level.
It counts the share of trades begun at a sign change of the hidden score that closed with a profit, and must be read with average win and loss because exits follow the engine's rule.

It is the hit rate of calling up when the normal-curve probability is at least one half; because the fit is unweighted, that cut reflects the training up share and the reference is the majority-class accuracy.
An unweighted probit can lean toward the side that was more common in training, and averaging the hit rate of the two sides shows whether its boundary separates them or merely follows that lean.
It condenses the four counts of called against actual direction into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the hidden score rarely crosses zero.
It grades the normal-curve probability on a bounded squared scale, so the result does not hinge on the few bars where the hidden score ran far into the curve's thin tails.

The fit is unweighted and nothing is fitted on validation bars, so the binned gap between the stated probability and the observed up share is a fair check of the probit's own odds, read with the count of occupied bins.
It checks the unit-variance noise assumed for the hidden score: a slope below one means the normal curve is turning the weighted sum into odds that are too bold on unseen bars.
The absolute-value penalty can set many weights to exactly zero, and the spread of the probability shows whether enough survived for the output to move away from the base rate.

Both logged numbers hold the plain logarithmic loss of the normal-curve probability, so their gap at the single step is a fair overfit check for this probit, although the absolute-value penalty the optimiser also paid for is in neither number.
It is the score on inner blocks of the training span that chose the penalty strength; it is a selection score, optimistic by construction, and not a result.

The fit is a single library call with no checkpoint choice; the single step reports the plain logarithmic loss of the probability of up on the training rows and on the validation rows, both without the penalty term, and selects nothing.

The adapter clips the probability to the closed range from zero to one, so a hidden score far in the tail can produce a probability of exactly zero or one and a very large logarithmic loss on that bar.

ridge_regression.summary: A straight-line fit of the coming move with an L2 penalty that keeps every weight small.
ridge_regression.implementationNote: Fitted on the price move; P(up) is read from its forecast through a logistic curve fitted on the validation bars.

penalty_strength.label: Penalty strength
penalty_strength.description: How hard the model is pushed toward small coefficients; larger is simpler.

native.produces: One number per bar, the expected value of a continuous target such as the coming price change, as a straight-line blend of the features whose weights are shrunk toward zero.
native.targetVariable: The expected size and sign of the coming continuous outcome, such as the price change over the horizon, given the bar's features
native.objectiveNote: Ridge adds a penalty on the squared size of the weights to least squares, which has a closed-form solution and shares weight among correlated indicators instead of letting them take huge opposite values.

metrics.why: Ridge solves for the weights that minimise squared misses, which aims the line at the average move, so the share of squared error it removes relative to forecasting no move is the fitted objective judged out of sample.
metrics.baseline: The mean squared actual move, which is the squared error of forecasting no move on the same resolved bars

metrics.why: It states the same squared-miss objective in points, so the typical size of the shrunk line's miss can be read against the typical size of a move.
metrics.baseline: The root mean square actual move on the same resolved bars, the error of forecasting no move

metrics.why: The absolute-error version is not what ridge minimises, but it shows whether the gain over forecasting no move survives when the few largest bars stop dominating the sum.
metrics.baseline: The mean absolute actual move on the same resolved bars

metrics.why: The penalty shrinks every weight, so the line's forecasts are deliberately too small; correlation ignores that shrinkage and asks only whether larger forecasts line up with larger realised moves.
metrics.baseline: Zero, no linear relation between forecast and realised move

metrics.why: The intercept is fitted on the training span's average move, so a drifting market shows up as a constant lean in the line that can pass for skill while the drift lasts.
metrics.baseline: Zero, no lean in either direction

metrics.why: The penalty strength is the single dial trading fit against stability, and the gap between squared error on validation rows and on training rows shows whether it was set too loose.
metrics.baseline: Zero, no gap between the two spans

notApplicable.name: Confidence Edge
notApplicable.why: The model has no class probability of its own to rank; natively the matching question, whether bigger forecasts go with bigger moves, is answered by the forecast-to-move correlation.

notApplicable.name: Brier Score

notApplicable.name: Brier score
notApplicable.why: Natively the shrunk line states a size of move and no probability of up, so there is nothing between zero and one to score; the curve fitted on validation bars is an as-run addition.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable model is a real ridge regression fitted in closed form on the volatility-scaled move over the horizon, as the specification describes, but the up or down call is not part of the specification: it comes from a logistic curve of the forecast fitted on the validation bars, so the probability metrics measure the shrunk line plus that curve.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is a two-parameter logistic curve applied to the ridge line's forecast of the scaled move, with the curve's slope and intercept fitted by maximum likelihood on the fold's validation bars only.

stepQuantity.unit: mean absolute error of the volatility-scaled horizon move, in scaled-move units and not in points, one value for the single fit; the training value is scored against the target clipped at extreme training percentiles and the validation value against the raw target

meaningful.why: Ridge minimises squared misses, which aims the line at the average move, so the share of squared error it removes relative to forecasting no move is its own objective judged on unseen bars.

quantile.description: Which quantile of the coming move the line fits; 0.5 is the median.

penalty_strength.label: Penalty strength
penalty_strength.description: How hard the model is pushed toward small coefficients; larger is simpler.

native.produces: A chosen percentile of the future value of the target for every bar, as a straight-line function of the bar's features, with a separate line fitted for each percentile wanted.
native.targetVariable: The stated percentile of the coming continuous outcome, such as the price change over the horizon, given the bar's features

metrics.why: The line is found by a linear programme that makes this tilted absolute miss as small as possible on training bars, so the same tilted miss on unseen bars is the only score that rewards landing on the chosen percentile and not on the average.
metrics.baseline: The pinball loss of quoting the training rows' unconditional quantile at the same level on every bar

metrics.why: A line fitted at a given quantile level promises that the realised move falls below it on that share of bars, and counting how often it really does tests the promise without reference to how far the misses were.
metrics.baseline: The quantile level the line was fitted at

metrics.why: When the level is set to one half the line is a median forecast, and the median is exactly what an absolute-error comparison against forecasting no move is consistent for.
metrics.baseline: The mean absolute error of forecasting no move on the same resolved bars
